item.title: Glutton for Punishment
item.description: Notes from a fast I didn’t finish
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
I’m a normal guy in a lot of respects. I like to workout, I think dogs are cool, I enjoy good movies. But there is one area I simply cannot downplay how absurdly great I am. Speed eating.

It’s more of a gift than a skill really. Ever since I can remember I’ve cleaned plates before my dining companion takes their second bite. In fact, the last time I sat down with someone who finished their food before me was 1999.

Since then, the gap between me and second place has only widened. People tell me things like “It’s not a race” and “Save some for me”, but I won’t hear it, that’s loser talk for people who expect sympathy for inadequacy.

Growing up, the scene in Ratatouille where Remy yells at Emile, “Don’t just hork it down!” was my family’s most recited quote. It was the signature battle cry to warn my siblings that I was serving myself thirds and that, if they wanted to eat, they needed to fight.

My reign continued for years until one day a group of friends invited me to join them for a 72 hour fast. They mentioned things like health benefits and mental clarity, but I couldn’t care less. I wanted to win and claim my title as master of both worlds, eating and not eating. If Michael Jordan took 2 years off to play baseball, I could take 3 days off to drink water and coffee.

Share

I kept journal entries of how I felt:

[Hour 0] It’s 6:30pm and I stuffed myself at dinner in fear of the impending fast. Clock starts now.

[Hour 18] starting to feel anxious. Normally, I’d walk a mile and eat a nice slop bowl for lunch. But now I have so much time to... do something else?

[Hour 20] wow so much of my day is dedicated to eating food, recovering from food, and planning what food to eat later. It’s like more than half the day.

[Hour 24] the group agreed we would walk together each day to help keep our minds off food. I feel calm, low energy, but not tired.

[Hour 26] we walked. I’m surprised at how long a group of people can talk about not doing something. Still, it was better than sitting alone and thinking about food.

[Hour 34] I am trying to write and I keep thinking, “oh that paragraph isn’t great, let me grab a protein bar and fix it”. As if the protein bar is a necessary ingredient in the act of writing better. It reminds me of how alcoholics describe their inner voice calling for booze. “If you drink a beer this morning, you won’t need one later”.

[Hour 36] It’s clear I use eating as emotional regulation. Now that I don’t have trail mix to numb myself, I have to actually feel the emotion. If my brain wants to feel bad about the shitty paragraph, I have to feel it rather than smother it with a snack.

[Hour 40] I use food like a baby uses a binky...

[Hour 48] the daily walk is coming at the perfect time today because I am getting that itch to use.

[Hour 49] I shared with the group that I, Dylan, am a food addict. I tell them I have been thinking about food all day long. I even bite the right inner side of my lip to mimic the sensation of it.

They look at me like I am crazy. Not eating wasn’t that big of a deal to them. “Just try not to think about it,” someone said, as if I hadn’t already thought about not thinking about it. I left the walk early and irritated. Night.

[Hour 61] my unconscious mind constantly says, “You should eat something because [insert reason here]”. It keeps trying different reasons. I can tell it is trained in the art of persuasion because it knows giving a reason, even a meaningless one, greatly increases compliance.

[Hour 63] I can’t focus at all

[Hour 64] neeeeed foooooooood

[Hour 65] going home, watching tv until this is done.

[Hour 65.5] tv boring, still can’t focus

[Hour 65.7] still boring

[Hour 65.8] I can’t take it anymore

The average time between thoughts about sustenance shortened from minutes to seconds. My inner-voice was persistent and unrelenting, and I feeble and wavering. My confident spirit had been zapped from my body like The Guy in Spy Kids.

In my weak state I folded, and at hour 66, I slumped into my slop bowl eating chair, my face colorless and knees weak, and ate two bowls to make up for lost time. The food restored my soul, then darkened it after I went too far.

In my semi-pleasurable food coma, I pondered how far I had come. Now that I lost, I decided winning was not everything. At hour 72, when everyone met for fast-breaking sushi, I stopped by, said hi, and left. I was happy for them, but hadn’t earned myself a seat. Minor league fasters don’t get championship sushi.

I’ve returned to my old speed eating ways with more perspective and a newfound respect for the other side. Fasting is tougher than I gave it credit for. Maybe one day I’ll try again, but for now I take solace in the fact that Michael Jordan wasn’t great at baseball either.

item.title: 1.5 Days in Court
item.description: How I Ended Up Testifying in a $50 Million Crypto Heist Trial
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
In September, a team of federal agents and prosecutors wanted to speak to me. My old roommate texted me a screenshot of an email he received from them.

“We have some reason to believe you, or someone in your household, may have been operating an Ethereum node during the timeframe of 2021 to 2023. - do you have a few minutes today to discuss that?”

My head was spinning with questions. What did they want with me? How did they come to this conclusion? Why was this coming from my old roommate?

“You are not in any way in trouble, we just need for technical reasons to prove that someone was operating a node in the geographic area of the Southern District of New York.”

Reading that line made me somewhat reassured. Running a node wasn’t illegal, but the government hadn’t always been friendly to crypto people. It felt like a situation where I could only lose, and I wanted no part of it.

Still, it was true. I had run a node in the past. It is a computer that stays on 24/7, runs software that keeps a copy of the blockchain, and works with other people’s nodes around the world to ensure transactions follow the rules. I was running one because I liked Ethereum, got rewards for doing it, and it helped me learn some new things.

Nervous about my own ignorance of the law, I made a few calls. My FBI agent friend assured me it wasn’t a scam. My lawyer friend informed me they were probably trying to “hook” me to testify at a trial. And my smart friend told me to ignore it. I didn’t owe these guys anything. Whatever they were doing was not my problem.

That advice was my favorite. I had already left New York 8 months prior. Now, I was between homes, visiting my grandma in California, and moving to Kazakhstan in two weeks. If I got wrapped up in this, it could hold me back indefinitely.

Ultimately, I lacked the guts to ghost the government. I scheduled the call and hoped I was one of dozens of guys who received that email. With any luck, they’d look at my situation, and pass.

I called in from my grandma’s swing set and said hi to the team. The prosecutor addressed me as Mr. Brodeur, and immediately I questioned my choice of makeshift office. Surely someone distinguished as Mr. Brodeur would never sit on a swing.

The prosecutor said his team was trying a guy who’d stolen over $50 million in crypto. They had the evidence, including a message where he bragged about pulling it off. What they were missing was something called venue, a rule written into the Constitution, which says that a crime has to be tried in the district where it occurred.

Venue came to be when Britain threatened to ship colonists across the ocean to be tried in England, far from their peers and any sympathetic jury. So in 1787, the Founding Fathers wrote venue into the Constitution to make sure that never happened.

But venue doesn’t make sense when applied to the internet and crypto. Crypto transactions, including the ones this guy used to take the money, happen everywhere and nowhere at once. Thousands of nodes around the world checked the same transactions mine did. But in the eyes of the law, mine was special because it was in the Southern District of New York, where I used to live, and where my node happened to be plugged in.

He went on to ask about the node. What kind of computer it was, the dates I ran it, and the building I lived in before confirming I was a fit. I tested my involvement one last time, “Are you asking me or telling me you need me for this?”

My captor smirked and kindly said, “You’d be surprised how hard it is to find someone who ran a node in a given area historically. We were actually worried he may get off on a technicality. If you stop responding or say no, we’ll subpoena you. Someone will come hand you a piece of paper that informs you that you need to come in. I’d prefer not to do that.”

I was curious how fast they could find me, but not curious enough to test it, and agreed to help.

I would have been less reluctant leading up to this had I felt my contribution was logical. My node didn’t make the defendant more or less guilty or provide any necessary data. This was rule following for the sake of rule following, and everyone involved knew it. The rule created to keep Americans out of court was dragging me into it. However, I couldn’t blame them for calling me in. Satisfying the rule is infinitely easier than amending the Constitution.

Knowing I had no choice, I felt relieved of the uncertainty and resolved to be as helpful as possible. He also said the testimony would likely land right before my flight to Kazakhstan, so nothing would be delayed.

Now that we were best friends, I felt comfortable asking how he found me.

They pulled IP addresses for nodes from Etherscan and matched them against Verizon’s addresses for the Southern District. This explained why he initially emailed my old roommate, who had set up the internet.

For years I’d listened to people rant about lack of online privacy, but never before had my internet footprint been tracked so blatantly. I felt simultaneously exposed and impressed.

We exchanged pleasantries and it was set. I was going to testify.

Two weeks later, I showed up to the courthouse, headed through the metal detectors, turned my phone in, and met one of the special agents who escorted me up to the 14th floor. The dark oak courtroom doors were looming, the kind you’d expect to see at Hogwarts. Behind them I could hear murmurs but nothing concrete.

To the right were two smaller doors with a metal placard between them that read “Witness Room.” They were closet-sized and windowless. I was told to wait until my name was called, and for the first time since high school, I experienced hours of true, uninterrupted, government-mandated boredom.

On the bright side, now that I was here, I knew for sure my move wasn’t getting delayed. It allowed me to look at it all as a unique experience. I wasn’t just staring at a wall. I was staring at a wall in court.

I was counting the small stars on the 1990s tan carpet when the special agent poked his head in to say “You’re up next” as if I needed to stop doing nothing to prepare to testify. This routine was repeated every hour or so, but with new phrases like “Almost there” and “Should be any minute now” before 5pm when he ultimately said, “We’re going to need you to come back tomorrow.”

Back again the next morning, I walked into the courthouse with a newfound swagger. “You know where you’re going?” the guard asked. “Yeah, this isn’t my first rodeo” I said. This time, I sat in the witness room for just a few minutes before my name was called.

I walked through those big doors and on the other side were 50 people staring directly at me. Everyone past the bar was playing a role in putting this guy away, and soon I would too. For two weeks I’d thought about this only in terms of me, but now I was seeing the bigger picture.

A woman at the opposite end of the room broke the silence and motioned for me to come towards the front. She had me take the oath and then my seat to the right of the judge.

The federal prosecutor, no longer a rectangle on a video call but an actual person, asked me to state my name and spell it. I learned that lawyers are very thorough when we started with groundwork questions: What is a blockchain? What is Ethereum? What does a node do?

Then came personal questions: When did you live in New York? Where? Did you run a node? They came as a barrage of smaller, simple-to-answer questions, but that’s what they added up to. I answered them all, telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

Cross-examination was simple, the defense attorney asked if I had any knowledge of the protocol or the man on trial. I didn’t, and I was dismissed. I’d been on the stand for maybe ten minutes.

To me, the contrast between crypto and court was clear. Crypto has a motto: “Don’t trust, verify.” There were plenty of ways to verify I’d run that node, but court didn’t need any of them. All I had to do was take an oath. Court’s motto might be “Don’t verify, trust.”

The special agent shook my hand, told me good job, and said I was free to go. I stepped out into a gray September day in my old neighborhood, travel plans intact. I felt proud of having done my civic duty and embarrassed that I’d tried to avoid it. No justice system is perfect, but ours works. And for 1.5 days, I got to be a small, procedural, necessary piece of it.

item.title: The Best Injury of My Life
item.description: A Short Story #5
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
“WHO THE FUCK IS 54?!” the varsity football coach roared. I froze and kept my head down because I, number 54, feared if I looked at him I would cry.

All 50 guys on the junior varsity defense were packed in our sweaty locker room watching film. We didn’t do this often, film time was better spent on varsity players, but Coach was looking for some undiscovered talent. Unfortunately, I was now both discovered and untalented.

Coach’s freakout started after we watched a play where I lined up in the wrong spot, and gave the other team’s running back a huge gap to score. It was a completely preventable mistake if I would just learn the plays.

While a simple task for most, memorizing plays felt overwhelming to me. The thought that I wasn’t a good player was uncomfortable and every time I opened that packet my heart rate would spike, my chest would tighten, and the voice in my head would incessantly tell me I was terrible. To combat this feeling, I resolved to avoid thinking about football whenever possible.

But now the thing I so desperately tried to escape was front and center. Coach smacked a metal locker and it reverberated as he raged, “THAT’S FUCKING AWFUL 54. WHO IS 54?” his eyes searched the room and I sank further in my chair.

Junior varsity had been big enough where one could hide and up to this point I was successful. But now, in this long drawn out silence, it seemed there was no avoiding it. Every second that passed increased the mounting embarrassment that would be sent my way.

Thankfully, God himself reached down and rang the school bell to save me from my public execution. We filed out of the room as coach snarled, “I WOULDN’T OWN UP TO THAT SHIT EITHER 54, IT’S FUCKING PATHETIC.”

I never returned.

The only reason I was on this team in the first place was because my parents forced me to be in a sport. I knew there would be punishment for quitting, but whatever it was, would not be as bad as crying in front of a room of teenage boys.

I decided to keep my quitting a secret for a few days while I figured out how to tell my parents. But this too would confront me sooner than I had hoped.

Football practice took up our lunch period and quitting meant I could leave campus to eat. One day, I went home to make a sandwich and was shaken when I saw my dad as I walked in. He was supposed to be at work, and I at practice. But here we were in the middle of the day, each pretending we were supposed to be there.

I feared immediate wrath, but none ever came. We had an enjoyable lunch and I went back to school, feeling odd but relieved about it.

He’d later tell me he’d been laid off and we’d need to move from Texas to Tennessee during the summer. I wouldn’t be punished but the understanding was once we moved I’d need to start football again.

I would’ve preferred to come in to Tennessee with zero expectations, but at 6’5 250 pounds, I was the perfect size for football. The coaches mistook size for ability and rolled out the red carpet for me. They let me pick number 80 after my favorite NFL player, gave me a new helmet reserved for the elite guys, and sent me to play tight end with the starters.

I enjoyed being treated this way, but it wouldn’t last long. At my first practice in pads, I dropped every ball. Five minutes after returning to the locker room, the coach came in, took number 80, and without saying a word, gave me 68.

I understood immediately. 68 was an offensive lineman’s number. Coach was telling me I was no longer a tight end. I was big and terrible, and that was where big, terrible people went.

I spent a month on the offensive line, where I was just as bad as I’d been before. Then, during a 1v1 blocking drill, I planted my foot in the mud and my knee folded under me like a closing laptop.

I hid my excitement when the doctor told me I was out for the season. I felt a severe knee injury was the best thing that could have happened to me. It got me out of playing without breaking my parents’ rule, and allowed me to larp as the player my new coaches first imagined. Now when people asked why I wasn’t playing, I could tell them I was injured instead of admitting I was bad.

As much as I would’ve liked to leave any mention of football behind me as I went to college, my size continued to invite the conversation. As a big guy, people love to ask you what sport you played, expecting to be dazzled with career highlights and stories about the Friday Night Lights.

Still insecure and desperate for approval, I would say “Yeah I played football but knee injuries ended my career”. My strategic ambiguity allowed me to tell the truth while deceiving the other person into thinking I was destined for great things before my horrible accident.

I always felt gross saying it. So here I am, confessing on Substack as penance for my half-truths.

Now when someone asks if I played football, I make sure to tell them I was terrible. I do this because they’re not asking if I spent four years on the bench, they’re asking if I was a star and got pussy.

Time has freed me enough from my embarrassment to share with the world, that I, 6’5 250 pound Dylan Brodeur, was not good at football and in fact, did not get pussy.

item.title: How to Give Gifts People Care About
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #103
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
I’ve received two great gifts recently.

(1) A leather book cover sized specifically for the type of journal I use. It’s expertly hand-stitched and has burnished edges. It is a pleasure to look at, touch, and smell every day.

(2) A bottle of Czereśniówka, a Polish liqueur our neighbor made and gave to my family. She told us the history and had us participate in the customary way of drinking it (shots before, during, and after dinner). The bottle has a custom label and was sealed in a way you would expect from a bottle at a store.

Some of the best gifts are things your recipient wants but can’t get themselves. While I can buy mass-produced liqueur and journal covers, I can’t buy the meaning behind these ones.

To know what your recipient wants, understand their problems and what they value. It helps to keep notes throughout the year on these things.

To give what your recipient can’t get themselves, draw on what you can offer that your recipient may not have.

  • Knowledge — Knowing something that helps you choose well, like if you have exceptional style

  • Access — Being able to get something the recipient couldn’t easily find or obtain, like buying things while in another country

  • Time & Effort — Putting work into finding, making, preparing, or presenting the gift

  • Skill — Bringing craftsmanship or expertise to what you give

  • Money — Spending resources to make the gift possible or add quality

The areas you combine give a gift its meaning. The book cover reflects time, effort, and skill honed over a lifetime of making. My neighbor’s knowledge and access to her Polish roots give the bottle a history that can be reflected on every time we drink it. I couldn’t have acquired either gift myself.

A common mistake is thinking gifts are things you have to buy because it’s what we do for children. Children find purchased gifts meaningful because they are broke. Once they can buy things themselves, the other elements matter more.

So to give good gifts, pay attention to what your recipient wants and can’t get, develop skills, and pay attention to the details. It could be as simple as giving freshly baked bread (as long as it’s good). Write some unique words along with it and wrap it to show you care.

In a world where so many items are soulless and uninspired, give the gift of meaning.

Sharing the blog is a double-whammy gift for me and whoever you share it with :)

item.title: The Art of Dogness
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #102
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
My dog Shiloh is getting old. Her coat is graying and a cloudiness fills her marble-like eyes. I’ve been lying on the floor with her and looking into them, reflecting on her life. Did she live a good one? Am I living a good one?

The discussion of what constitutes a “good life” has been going on for 2.5 thousand years. Although it seems important to everybody, we never discussed it in school but for one day in Philosophy 101.

Despite being such an old topic, there is still much disagreement. Some say life is about maximizing pleasure, others argue it is about realizing your potential, some views are religious, others are nihilist. Perhaps we are too close to life to definitively say what makes a good one.

But once we stop talking about our own lives and start talking about dogs, we find some consensus.

All can agree a bad life for a dog is one locked in a cage all day and ignored. To do this to a dog is to rob him of his dogness. The part of him that wants to play in a field or socialize cannot be exercised in this cruel caged life.

Conversely, a good life for a dog is one where he can express lots of dogness, free to roam around and do dog things.

We are confident in saying this because we understand the dog’s reality. We have closely observed good and bad dog lives. They do not need to maximize pleasure or accept God as their one true lord and savior. Yet if we apply the same logic to ourselves, we often reject the idea that it could be so simple.

But what if it is? What if the key to a good life is to express lots of humanness?

Humanness means living according to our inner nature.

As a human, you desire some amount of social interaction, outside time, and movement. Beyond these universal urges, you have some unique to you. Certain activities, places, people, and problems pull at you more than others. You feel drawn toward some things for reasons you can not fully explain.

These desires are encoded inside you. Studies of animals raised in isolation found that beavers still build dams and spiders still spin webs. No one had to teach these animals to do these things, it is encoded in them as humanness is in us.

Unfortunately, many disregard their humanness, pushing it down in the name of pleasing others, because the #1 regret of the dying is “I wish I’d had the courage to live a life true to myself, not the life others expected of me.”

In our quest for approval, we cage ourselves with other people’s expectations. We seek to please, avoid looking foolish, and wear a mask pretending to be somebody else.

This strategy may have worked well in the past, but sucks if you live in 2026. You won’t die if some people don’t like you and people will actually like you more for your authenticity.

I’ve spent my fair share of time in cages of my own making. I’ve worked at companies because other people thought they were prestigious, continued to date people to avoid disappointment, and pretended to share opinions to fit in.

But it’s never too late change. I’m doing things like moving to Kazakhstan and writing full-time. People think I’m fucking crazy but my intuition tells me it’s right for me.

As I scratch Shiloh, tufts of her hair float around and her stink transfers to my hand. It’s cool though, because the look on her face tells me she thinks life is good and I do too.

item.title: Why I'm Moving to Kazakhstan & You Should Too
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #101
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Fuck New York City, I’m moving to Borat’s hometown.

Well not his hometown, but Astana, KZ, a place that I admittedly knew nothing about last month. My incorrect assumption was that Kazakhstan was a place of dirt roads, livestock, and villages, but it actually looks incredibly futuristic.

Obviously where you live is a big decision. It determines who you are by determining who you are around. So who’s in Kazakhstan?

The Network School (NS).

It’s is a co-living community of people from all walks of life. Many of the people are founders, creators, and business owners, so there is lots of interesting conversations. Members host all kinds of events where they share skills they’re uniquely good at, like yoga or coding. It has a real generous culture of contributing to the tribe.

I lived at NS earlier this year when it was based in Malaysia and loved it. Initially I planned to be there for just a few months but ended up committing for a year+. I love that everything is handled for me and I can just lock in, I love that I can just come downstairs to hangout with anybody, and I love that it gets me out of my comfort zone.

Network School makes it easy to visit by providing all meals and living arrangements for you. It’s a high quality of life for $1,500/mo (rent, meals, electricity, and gym all included).

They do visits as short as one month, use my referral, and check it out with me.

Pamela Anderson would want you to share.

item.title: The Tractor of Our Time
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #100
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
The story The Grapes of Wrath follows a family that was kicked off the farm they had worked on for 3 generations. Although fictional, the story talks about a real starvation crisis that affected tenant farmers after manual labor was made obsolete by the tractor in the early 1900s.

These displaced farmers, unsure where to direct their hunger fueled hatred, hated the tractor, its operator, the landowner, the lenders, and its shareholders. But it was of no use, none of them were the monster behind their unemployment.

The monster, as Steinbeck called it, was the bank. In its insatiable need for profit, it caused human suffering along the way. And even though no particular banker wanted to evict the farmers, the need for profit demanded it. The bank was made by man, but man could not control it.

A century later, it’s easy for us to look at their pain and be grateful. It was a price paid for a freedom we enjoy today. This monster was an evolutionary pressure that freed us to work easier and more lucrative jobs as the share of US workers in agriculture fell from 41% to 2% from 1900 to 2000.

But there is no stop button on evolution, and the tractor of 1939 sounds a lot like AI of 2026.

The same monster that ate tenant farming will eat many kinds of jobs. It will be messy, it will be unfair, it will happen fast, and it wont stop. The monster must eat.

People will hate AI, its creators, and the VCs for the labor they replace. But these are the same people would have hated the tractor in 1939, unable to see beyond today, demanding the ever-changing world stay the same.

Help the tractor find its next field. Help the blog find its next friend.

item.title: Rhetoric Needs a Rebrand
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #99
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
The great quotes of history didn’t just happen to be great, they were engineered that way.

To understand why, you first have to understand how humans remember things.

The human is an information glutton, constantly consuming and looking for more. But we have limited storage, so we maximize the amount we can know by compressing information using patterns. We pattern match by associating new things we want to remember with old things we already know. Even the world’s best memorizers do this, just much better than us.

Great writers know people use patterns for memorization, so they build pattern into their most important lines, making the reader’s job easy.

The study of patterns in language is called rhetoric, and there are fewer patterns than you might think. Classical English Rhetoric, one of the best-known books on the subject, lists just 22.

My two problems with the existing rhetoric literature are

  1. Whoever named the different patterns gave them stupid technical names like Epistrophe and Anaphora. How are people supposed to remember that? Those names are in direct conflict with what the study of rhetoric is all about.

  2. They mainly study text that is 300+ years old. This isn’t inherently bad, we just talked differently back then, so it’s less useful for someone trying to utilize rhetoric today.

So I picked a few of my favorite quotes, teased apart the rhetoric tools that make them great, and renamed the tool.

1. The Parallel

“That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”— Neil Armstrong

Armstrong delivered this line at the pinnacle of humanity’s greatest achievement (walking on the moon), so you might say this line has an unfair boost in notoriety.

But also, no one would quote this if he said, “I’m walking on the moon, this is important for us.” In that way, clarity and conciseness are necessary, but not sufficient, for great communication.

Armstrong gives the two parts of the sentence the same frame. Five words on each side, repeating two and a half of the words.

one small step for man
one giant leap for mankind

Repeating the “man” in “mankind” gives the line a pleasing sense of sameness between the literal man and the conceptual mankind.

The line also delivers a strong metaphor to align pro-gress, as in man moving forward, and prah-gress, as in mankind advancing.

We love repetition, we love metaphors, we love progress, we love this quote.

2. The Reverse

“Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.”
— John F. Kennedy

The reverse is like the parallel but flipped. The same words are repeated on both sides of the sentence, but to point out an error instead of sameness.

your country → you
you → your country

The reverse is helpful for surprising the reader, it works when you’re rejecting something that is generally felt to be true. In this case, people look to the government to provide them things and JFK says, “No, you!”

Charlie Munger often repeated the advice, “Invert, always invert.” (which also uses repetition). That premise is useful when using the reverse.

3. The Arc

“Civilization begins with order, grows with liberty, and dies with chaos.”
— Will and Ariel Durant, The Lessons of History

The arc is perhaps our most familiar pattern.

The beginning, middle, and end
The introduction, body, and conclusion
The birth, life, and death.

The arc follows the rule of three, which is the idea that things presented in groups of three tend to feel more memorable, satisfying, and complete. Three is the smallest number that can create a complete journey. One thing is just a thing, two things is a thing comparison, but three things is a story. And in the quote above, Will and Ariel Durant give us the concise story of all civilizations using 3 words in each of the 3 parts.

4. The Cycle

“Hard times create strong men. Strong men create good times. Good times create weak men. And weak men create hard times.”
— G. Michael Hopf

The cycle is a lot like the arc, except it bends back to the beginning. A good cycle will connect so cleanly that nothing feels unresolved.

Cycles feel familiar because we live them. Day and night, the seasons, the economy, and life all follow cycles. These cycles are just patterns that become more visible when you zoom out.

Hopf combines the cycle pattern with repetition to make this quote memorable. You only need to remember the quote starts with “Hard times,” and logic carries you through the rest, each phrase knocking into the next like a row of dominoes.

5. The Stairs

“I’m a libertarian at the national level, a Republican at the state level, a Democrat at the municipal level, and a socialist at the family level.”— Nassim Nicholas Taleb

Taleb shares the surprising idea that someone can be both a libertarian and a socialist. It is surprising because we don’t normally use political labels to describe how someone runs a family. The surprise makes it memorable, but the structure makes it memorizable.

The structure is like a staircase, as the scale of government descends down, his tolerance for control ascends up. Much like the cycle, you only need to remember that Taleb starts at the top of the stairs to follow the pattern of revealing the rest.

There are many more patterns I could explore, perhaps in a future WIBTAL. But one thing feels clear. How you say something is just as important as what you say. Take away the repetition from these quotes, or add a word that breaks the rhythm, and they become immediately less memorable.

Ask not what this blog can do for you—ask what you can do for this blog. Share it.

Share

item.title: Getting Coffee With Younger Me
item.description: A Short Story #5
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
It has been 5 years since I moved to New York City. When I think about that guy who took the leap from Tennessee, it’s hard to believe we are the same person.

I wonder what it would be like to get coffee with him. I wonder in what areas he’d be relieved and which disappointed. I wonder what he’d resent me for and what would surpass his wildest dreams.

He’d probably ask what our biggest changes are, expecting to hear how much money we made or places we traveled, but neither would cross my mind. Assuming it wouldn’t change the past, these are the changes I’d tell him he can look forward to:

You Develop a Reverence for Makers

You haven’t yet learned how hard it is to make things. All you know is competing for existing jobs at existing companies managed by people who took your same path. You are playing house in the home a maker built.

Luckily, you get to meet some great makers along the way, but even then, you won’t understand what it takes until you try it for yourself.

Inspired by your maker friends, you will create products and projects of your own. Most will fail, but through failure you develop the eyes to see. Every entrepreneur, regardless of size and success, will earn your respect because they are the ones building the world around you.

You Put The Goal Above the System

I know you love habits, it is true that you they were instrumental in changing you from an undisciplined shirk to someone with focus, but you will take it too far.

Your journal will fill entire pages with all the current health and productivity trends you wish to do daily. Things like: cold showers, gratefulness, affirmations, stretching, and supplements.

These pages contain things that are ‘good’ for you but it irks you when you miss a day and really upsets you when you miss two. You will look at your system and wonder, what is this all for?

Eventually, you admit defeat and accept you can’t do everything. You declare habit bankruptcy and now only keep a few that help support your health and writing.

We Want to Write

One day, you will be at the museum with a few friends, and you will be sooo bored. You will look around and see creations of great skill and dedication, but lament that it’s just not your thing.

The thing you will take away is how your friend Aurora floated around the museum in a state of bliss. She found intricacies in every painting we looked at and you could tell she loved every moment. “How do I get like her?” you will wonder for years.

In your own life you will read books and and excitedly tell people about them. You will see them mentally check out of the conversation. You will bore people with quotes and concepts. But you will realize, good books are your museum.

After this realization, you decide there is no effort as worthy as trying to be a writer yourself, and that being a not-great, broke writer is better than a rich anything else.

Younger Dylan might resist the Maker and System points, certain he knows better than his future self. But when I tell him about becoming a writer, I think he would smile. I have always carried journals and used writing to find clarity, it just felt impractical to treat it as anything more than a private habit. But, luckily for me, becoming a Maker meant not letting practicality determine what I do.

Share this post to get coffee with Younger Dylan

Share

item.title: Token White Guy
item.description: A Short Story #4
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
My professor designated me the token white guy of my class because I was the only one who fit all 3 criteria of the woke’s unholy trinity: white, straight, and male. Unlike token black guys, they didn’t use pictures of me on the university website to give the appearance of diversity. Rather, they used me as a punching bag.

The course was called “Leadership Studies,” and I took it because I wanted to be a leader, just like my dad. I wasn’t sure how someone attained the ability to lead, so I figured taking a course on it would be the best way to learn. The longer the course went on, however, the less it seemed to have anything to do with its name.

All too often, the professor would bring in politically charged conversations and we’d just talk. “How is this person being a leader?” was a common question which received insultingly obvious responses for a thing you pay money to attend.

One day I remember in particular was the day we discussed cultural appropriation. The conversation centered around the white girl who went viral for wearing a Chinese dress to her prom.

“I don’t see a problem with it, she likes the style,” I said

The girl next to me turned red and her neck veins raged, “WHAT THE ACTUAL FUCK—ARE YOU KIDDING ME? THIS IS A TEXTBOOK MANIFESTATION OF WHITE PRIVILEGE AND THE COMMODIFICATION OF MARGINALIZED CULTURES. YOU DO NOT GET TO EXTRACT THE LABOR OF AN OPPRESSED PEOPLE, DETACH IT FROM ITS HISTORICAL TRAUMA, AND REPURPOSE IT FOR YOUR OWN PERFORMATIVE SELF-EXPRESSION.”

I sat there while the girl tore into me, spittle flying in my direction. I remember thinking, “Is the professor going to offer me any support here?” But no, she let it go on and on. Then she got the opinion of others in the class, all of which agreed with the girl. White girl after white girl made subtle disses at me as to how my privilege was so great that I couldn’t even see the hardship the rest of the world felt.

I was ashamed of myself. The consensus was clear, the real leaders were the people on social media “educating” the girl on why she should not wear the dress. “Obviously, if I’m the only person who thought this way, I must be wrong” I thought. I even apologized for my ignorance to the whole class. It was a real life Asch conformity experiment and it worked.

Later that year, the professor gave us a packet about Sweatt v. Painter. It was a Supreme Court case where Heman Sweatt, a Black man, was rejected from the all-white University of Texas Law school because of his race.

The professor then said she wanted to role-play the trial. She asked the girl from the dress incident to be Sweatt’s attorney (good guy) and me to be Painter’s attorney (racist piece of shit). No script, just talk as you think these people would.

I knew this was bad news bears from the start but I was too scared of authority to say anything. Again, this was leadership studies, not acting, not history, not law. She was intentionally setting me up for a spanking for being token white guy.

Girl: “Your honor, my client is qualified to attend the University of Texas Law school and was rejected because of his race. This is unjust. I demand that my client be admitted to the institution at once.”

Me: “So the uhh... University of Texas doesn’t think that uh... black people should be allowed here because they... don’t fit in.”

Her: “SO YOUR POSITION IS THAT A QUALIFIED BLACK MAN SHOULD BE EXCLUDED FROM THE SCHOOL BECAUSE WHITE PEOPLE LIKE YOU DON’T WANT HIM SITTING BESIDE THEM?”

Whoa. That seemed personal? Okay just stay in character.

Me: Well I mean, black people are uhh... better off in a separate place I think

Her: “YOU’RE LITERALLY DEFENDING SYSTEMIC RACISM! YOUR WHITE PRIVILEGE IS BLINDING YOU FROM THE FACT THAT SEPARATE ACCESS IS NOT EQUAL ACCESS TO OPPORTUNITIES. MY CLIENT WOULD BE DENIED THE SAME ACCESS AS WHITE STUDENTS. YOU CANNOT CLAIM THE RESULT IS EQUAL.”

I looked toward the professor the same way I would look at my dad when I was getting ‘the belt’, begging for it to stop.

Me: Uhh...

Her: “THIS CASE IS NOT ABOUT EDUCATIONAL POLICY. IT IS ABOUT WHITE SUPREMACISTS USING THE LAW TO KEEP BLACK PEOPLE OUT OF WHITE INSTITUTIONS. PEOPLE LIKE YOU ARE THE PROBLEM WITH THIS WORLD!!!”

I looked away from the professor and at the girl. Her eyes burned with rage, all of her social justice activism had prepared her for this moment.

Seconds pass and the room gets increasingly tense waiting for my reply. I tell the professor that I’m uncomfortable continuing and she let us stop. The girl’s fury transformed into a smug grin, proud of her victory, as though she just delivered the Emancipation Proclamation and freed the slaves.

I felt heavy for the rest of class, carrying a tremendous amount of shame. As soon as we were dismissed I left without talking to anyone, walking at a fast pace so as to not be seen, head down, defeated.

I only recognized what this was a few years later. A humiliation ritual, with me as the scapegoat, designed to insert guilt into my soul, put on for the enjoyment of those that detested the white man, professor included.

All of this being said, I don’t blame anybody but myself. I could have had an opinion on what a good Leadership Studies class looked like and once that standard had not been met, I could’ve dropped it. Instead, I outsourced my thinking, letting credentials convince me someone knew better.

So in a way, Leadership Studies taught me the most important lesson I would learn in college, the importance of thinking for myself. As with all great lessons, it came with pain. A pain that ensures I won’t forget its importance.

At least now I can laugh. Laugh at the fact that this professor had a PhD, a thing I used to think meant something. Laugh at woke culture, a thing that we used to let dominate what we could and couldn’t say. And laugh at the irony, that these people convinced me a Chinese dress was racist, but that dressing me up in a gimp suit wasn’t.

item.title: The Four Quadrants of Communication
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #98
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
A statement can be literally false and not dishonest. A statement can also be technically true while creating a false impression. Therefore, intent determines honesty more than accuracy.

That distinction forms the basis of what I call the Four Quadrants of Communication.

4 Quadrants of Communication

The quadrants classify individual statements, not people. The colors reflect how I feel when I receive each type from someone that I have an ongoing relationship with and therefore expect a reasonable degree of honesty.

They are not universal moral judgments, rather, it’s just a silly little chart.

Hyperbole

Hyperbole is deliberate and obvious exaggeration used for emphasis, emotion, or humor. It is not intended to be understood as fact.

  • “I’m starving”

  • “I’ve told you a million times.”

  • “This bag weighs a ton.”

While these phrases are literally false, their intended meanings are easy to understand. Mostly harmless, but sometimes annoying, so still think it’s best to be literal. Okay

Truth

I like truth, especially when it is unpleasant. The more someone is willing to tell me unpleasant truthful things, the more pleasant I find our relationship. Good

Lying

I hate lies, especially casual ones. A casual lie signals that you are willing to manipulate another person’s perception, even when the stakes are low. Bad

Strategic Ambiguity

Strategic ambiguity is the deliberate use of multiple possible interpretations, allowing the speaker to later deny one of them.

  • “Per my last email” means, “Apparently, you are an idiot and can not read”

  • “He’s an interesting guy” means “I don’t like him”

  • “Does this dress look okay?” means “Please reassure me that I am attractive”

The ambiguity is strategic because it allows the sender to claim a different intention depending on response.

  • Email sender can claim they were just pointing you in the right direction, even though they metaphorically spit on you

  • Commenter can claim they never said anything bad about the guy because they used a positive sounding word

  • Girl can claim to herself that she was just wondering about the dress because directly asking for a compliment devalues it

Strategic ambiguity transfers the risk of communication from the speaker to the listener. The speaker gets to imply something without owning it while the listener has to decide what was really meant.

These statements are not inherently bad, but repeated strategic ambiguity signals a low-trust relationship where the speaker is continually placing the burden of interpretation on the listener. Ideally, a relationship should trend towards less and less ambiguity over time. Bad.

I won’t lie: I would love if you shared

item.title: How I got into the Hall of Shame
item.description: A Short Story #3
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
October’s pleasant autumn air stood in stark contrast to the dread I felt working in public accounting. Every morning, I woke up feeling as though another piece of my soul had been eaten by the corporate-interest machine. My life wasn’t all bad, I got to live in New York City after all, but I needed to escape if I wanted to maintain my sanity.

My firm had just kicked me off an important banking client and demoted me to a team that audited regional gas stations. I wanted to be good, but I couldn’t help it, I was bored as fuck and it showed in my work.

On top of being bad at my job, “Busy Season” was only a few months away, it was the time of year when 12-hour days were expected. I absolutely loathed working 8 hours, so 12 seemed unbearable. But I was broke and in student debt, so I needed another job to jump to if I was going to avoid this giant rolling boulder Indiana Jones-style.

I must have been at the top of LinkedIn’s filter for burned-out and desperate because my inbox was flooded with recruiters. Unfortunately, their spam DMs offered only slightly less terrible versions of the same job I already had.

I worried that if I took one and left after only a few months, the rat-race gods would press a scalding-hot iron into my forehead and brand me JOB HOPPER, forever banishing me to corporate hell where my only remaining career path would be Costco greeter.

So I copy-pasted a response to all of them that said:

“Not interested in this job, but if you have anything in crypto let me know”

Crypto was the only thing that could hold my attention. My naïveté about the world, crypto’s rapid rise, and my urge to bet it all combined into the perfect dopamine cocktail for my 24-year-old male brain.

Of the hundred recruiters I messaged, only 2 replied. Pickings were slim, so I knew I’d have to interview well.

I got on a phone call with one recruiter and after a few pleasantries, he asked, “Say, are you related to Martin Brodeur?”

I got this question a lot, especially from late-20s white guys in the Northeast like this recruiter. Martin Brodeur was a Hall of Fame goalie for the New Jersey Devils. When hockey fans learned my last name is also Brodeur, they were quick to ask.

“Haha, yeah. You mean Uncle Marty?” I joked, despite having no relation to the man whatsoever.

His eyes went wide.

“Oh my God. Dude, that’s insane!”

This is the point I usually tell the recipient that I’m kidding, but this guy was so enthusiastic about, that I didn’t have a chance.

“I had his jersey growing up. His poster was on my wall. I watched every Devils game with my dad.”

I opened my mouth to tell him it was a joke, but he barreled through me.

“Brodeur is literally the reason I played goalie, he was my favorite player.”

Now I felt bad, this guy wasn’t even stopping to breathe and I needed to tell him the truth pronto.

“I can’t wait to tell my dad I met Marty Brodeur’s nephew.”

Shit. Too late.

“hah, yeah,” I said. “...pretty crazy!”

I got on this call wanting a job but now I would have given anything to get off it.

I listened to the recruiter tell me about opportunities I wouldn’t consider for a second out of fear that my parasitic lie would transfer to the people working there. I was stern in expressing my disinterest to justify ghosting him later.

The call went on and I could feel the words to tell him the truth in my chest, but like a 7th grade boy at the school dance, I couldn’t muster the courage to say anything.

“I’ve got this one job over by where your Uncle lives, you ever go over there?”

“Yeah we do Sunday dinners sometimes.” I shot my hand through my hair and grabbed a fist full of it, silently mouthing the words WHAT THE FUCK to tell myself I was mad at me for telling a 2nd lie.

I got off the call as soon as I could and felt some relief. No harm no foul, right?

The next day, my phone buzzed over and over with his calls and texts. I expected a follow-up but this was next level. He really wanted to help Martin Brodeur’s nephew get a job.

A number I didn’t recognize calls and I pick up.

“Hey Dylan, this is So-and-so, I’m the CEO of the recruiting company” My heart sinks, “I heard your story, super awesome that you’re related to Martin Brodeur. How are you doing?”

His seasoned voice intimidated me, never before had important business people wanted to talk to me, “Hah.... yeah.. Doing pretty well.”

“Well hey listen I just got off the phone with a friend, the Chief Accounting Officer at Coinbase. She’s excited about you, I think we can get you a job there with a salary bump and equity.”

My gut did a somersault. Coinbase was the best company I could’ve asked for, an oasis compared to the barren hellscape I was working in. But under no circumstances could I take this job. Surely this was divine punishment for my fabrication.

“Just shoot your resume over and we’ll get you that interview”

“Sure thing”

click

“FUUUUUUUUUCK.”

I lay on my hardwood floor, staring at the ceiling for so long that I began to feel the Earth rotating beneath me. I ruminated for hours on how I could somehow thread the needle between “Sorry I lied” and “Can I still get that job?”

The next day, texts poured in from the CEO. I ignored them, silently begging the devil to free me from his temptation.

I could have told him the truth. I played it out in my head repeatedly. Even if it killed my chance at the Coinbase job, at least my conscience would be clear and I could prevent any future misunderstanding.

Instead, I employed a 3rd lie to end my suffering. I texted him that I would be taking an offer from another company. An offer that, like Uncle Marty, did not exist.

I still wonder what would have happened had I found the strength to call the CEO and tell him the truth. Maybe he would have rightfully felt manipulated. Maybe he would have laughed.

Instead, I kept the lie alive because I felt I couldn’t endure a few minutes of awkwardness. I chose to lie to two men I’d never speak to again in order to protect their opinion of me.

Fortunately, I eventually got a different job in crypto, one that was great to me and opened many doors. I got it through the other recruiter who responded to me on that first day.

Ironically, he also asked me if I was related to Martin Brodeur. Perhaps I hadn’t learned my lesson because I still made my dumb Uncle Marty joke. But this time, after hearing his voice perk up, I quickly cut him off and told him the truth.

item.title: Think like a Scientist, Communicate like a Storyteller
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #97
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Ray Rice, a former star running back for the Baltimore Ravens, was arrested in February 2014 after he punched his fiancée unconscious in an elevator.

The NFL conducted an investigation and, with all of the relevant information, decided that a 2-game suspension was appropriate. The suspension would cost him over $500k in missed games and fines.

For the months following, things were normal. Rice continued to practice with the team in preparation of the 3rd game of the season. However, in September 2014, the full video of Rice knocking her out surfaced. The Ravens immediately cut him, the NFL increased his suspension, and he would never play again.

There was nothing in the video that wasn’t in the investigation, but our experience of the facts changed. Watching her head jolt to the right and seeing her body smack against the handrail made the world respond differently than it had to the words.

Vision is our most visceral sense. We experience what we see more intensely than what we hear or read, that intensity changes what we believe. Videos of bombings on the news will incite people more than reading the newspaper description of it. Also, I can tell you about an injury to a pro athlete without issue, but you might turn away when the slow motion replay comes on.

This matters because if we only react strongly to things when we see them, we will miss important facts, even when they can save lives.

In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that mothers were dying far more often when doctors delivered babies than when midwives did. He ordered doctors to wash their hands after autopsies and deaths during labor fell from 18% to 2%.

Armed with data, he took his finding to the hospitals, journals, and medical societies of Europe, excited to save lives of mothers everywhere. But doctors mostly rejected his idea. In the 18 years that Semmelweis yelled and screamed to wash your hands people never listened. They couldn’t see the germs that were killing mothers, so they didn’t believe they were real.

Semmelweis never lived to see his vindication, but in 1864, Louis Pasteur showed microscopic life caused disease. He left two flasks of broth open to the air, one shielded from microbes and one exposed. The exposed spoiled while the shielded stayed clear. This was evidence of germs that people could see. Soon after, Pasteur’s findings were applied to surgery and by the 1870s, handwashing was a standard medical practice.

So in both cases with Ray Rice’s domestic abuse punishment and Semmelweis’ call for handwashing, it was seeing that changed people’s perspectives.

We all know the idioms “Seeing is believing” and “A picture is worth a thousand words,” but I don’t think they are quite right.

“Seeing is believing” describes most, but not all. Semmelweis believed the numbers with no picture to go on.

“A picture is worth a thousand words” is wrong too. No number of words describing the Rice incident would have the impact that the video did. In this way, a picture/video is worth more than words can buy.

So what does this mean for our lives?

1. Our eyes can lie to us, so we should think like scientists
If you only believe what you can see, you’ll continually misjudge the world. You’ll overvalue anecdotes and viral videos while undervaluing statistics, trends, and invisible forces. You will miss the germ theory like the mother killing doctors.

2. Facts aren’t persuasive, so we should communicate like storytellers
Semmelweis died in an insane asylum because he was yelling at people instead of telling them a story. If he has done the work around finding the underlying reasons of the death and shown people germs, he would have been much more persuasive and successful.

Subscribe to not beat your fiancée in an elevator

item.title: All You Can Eat part 2
item.description: A Short Story #2
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Group by group the giants slunk out the door. Chairs are stacked. Blinds are let down. The clatter fades before a final flick and the world returns to darkness when our day begins.

Our kind has to wait for darkness to explore and find food because the giants persecute us on site. You see, the giants are bigots, picking and choosing the species they want to live and die on whim. We unfortunately catch the latter.

The fish however, get a glass palace where they are fed straight into their mouths. Spending their days philosophizing while we have to hide in the walls and under the floor in a constant state of war and famine.

We tried diplomacy. My own father, a popular social justice activist in the colony, organized a crawl for the cause. Roach Lives Matter, he called it. While the giants ate, he and 22 others crawled in protest of the giants cruelty.

They crawled from the chewed-out floorboard in the sparsely used mop closet onto the open plain of off-white tile. A thin sticky film coated the ground and one-by-one marched over it into the dining area.

My dad was the bravest roach I’ve ever known, but what he possessed in courage he lacked in judgement. He presumed their numbers would help the giants perceive the error of their ways. Their presence was met with a piercing screech, a war call, prompting the entire staff to attack and end the peaceful protest.

I watched from the small split in the door frame of the mop closet. Everyone on the floor scattered in different directions but my eyes were fixated on my dad. I wanted to scream as I saw a rather unfashionable black non-slip sneaker come crashing down on him.

SMACK! His flat oval shape body absorbed much of the contact, as he was still alive when the shoe lifted. The look in his eyes immediately shifted from “panicked” to “freaking the fuck out”.

WHAM! He’s hit again. The shoe rose but he was still going, this time slower than before. The bonk broke his left antennae and with it, his instinct to survive. You could tell at this point he wasn’t sure where he was anymore.

The giant warrior’s final blow was slow and deliberate. He planted the sole of his sketcher squarely on the my father’s head and twisted. A sharp crunch echoed through the room as his exoskeleton gave way and he was smeared across the cold tile floor.

The room calmed but my gaze hadn’t shifted. My dad’s legs twitched in the air fueling my disbelief that he was dead. Impossible, I thought, as a broom swept him away and with it my boyhood belief that he was invincible.

3 out of the 23 made it back alive, but it would prove pointless to count the death toll as the massacre was only beginning.

The next day a big white vehicle with an image of an upside down roach and lightning bolts striking on it parked outside. What a silly image, I thought, we hardly go outside so why would we get struck by lightning.

A giant who was shorter than most hopped down from his booster seat and unloaded his weapons of mass destruction from the back before entering.

A menacing grin appeared on his face that could only come from the fulfillment of a perverted desire. His smile displayed rotting teeth and slightly lifted his black mustache that was no wider than his nose. He covered his grin with a mask that protected himself from the pain he inflicted on us.

Deadly gas filled The Premium Chinese Buffet, all around me I watched my friends and family lose coordination and stand paralyzed against their will. The fumes hijacked their minds and when I touched antennas with them, could tell their souls had been stolen, leaving behind hollow husks suspended mid-step.

More than two-thirds of us succumbed to the gas. Those of us who survived appeared to possess a resistance to the poison that had inflicted such agony on the colony.

I should feel lucky, but I can’t help wish I died with them. My father got to die a martyr but I live with the consequences.

Everyone turns away when they see me coming. No one will touch antennas with me. They look at me with disgust as if I was the one who gassed their family.

I’m so alone.

item.title: Pay to Pray
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #96
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Thailand’s monks would make killer startup founders.

I recently went on a group tour to visit different Buddhist temples and look at sun-beaten statues of their gods. Some had elephant trunks for noses, others had 10 arms, but each one was hundreds of feet tall.

In front of every statue was a donation box. The monks stressed the importance of giving to each one because the gods had different powers. Give to this one for good sex. Give to that one to lose weight.

The gods must really know their target market because those boxes were full of cash from all over the world. The West sells you drugs to help you look and fuck better but the monks sell divine intervention. Same base desires, just different solutions.

If the gods were unworthy of your hard-earned dollars, you could always buy goods from the monk run trinket shops outside the temples. Here you could find things such as weed grinders that say “I Phucking Love Thailand” and penis shaped bottle openers. Their product choice likely informed by demand rather than Buddhist principles.

In the van on our way back, a young European on the tour says to me that he was uncomfortable with so many monks prompting him for money. “Aren’t these supposed to be holy places?” he said, suggesting that the sacred way to ask for money is passing a felt-lined wicker basket up and down pews.

Faith may be free but church is a business. I respond that they have to make money somehow. The monk’s directness comes from a deep understanding of their customers. They know they’ll never see us again, that we have more money than the locals, and that we feel guilty for how fortunate we are to not be them. The slow, no-pressure approach his hometown church uses is just a method for a different kind of customer. One better suited for people you’ll keep seeing on Sundays.

I continue sharing my analysis on the business model of temple tourism, using jargon like “diversifying revenue” and “customer churn”. His eyes glaze over and I can feel his desire to exit our conversation in favor of silence among exhausted strangers.

I turn and press my forehead to the moist van window and think about my day. I didn’t know what to expect from the monks, but I left convinced they’re hardcore, living the principles so many entrepreneurs only talk about. They’d never use the fancy words I did to describe their business, but they live them better than I ever have.

Subscribe to lose weight and have good sex.

item.title: All You Can Eat
item.description: A Short Story #1
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Every morning starts the same with a jingle jangle outside the front door and a collection of flicks that return brightness to the world. We live in a building called the “Premium Chinese Buffet”. There are many of us here, more than there should be considering the amount of space we have. I have never counted the total because it would be impossible to keep everyone still for that long and I don’t really have the attention span for that.

As my eyes start adjusting to the abrupt return of light I’m reminded how filthy it is in here, I’m surprised that the feeders partake in their own eating here after seeing our pond has to be indicative of how their kitchen looks.

The highlight of every day is when the feeders bless us with food. Every day they give us these delicious hard brown dusty pellets retrieved from the red box. The feeder will insert a coin into the box and spin the handle. click crrrk crrrk tap tap tap tap tap, its a sweet sound that can be heard above all the clatter of a restaurant, kind of like how you can hear your name over the noise of a crowded room. The delicious sustenance hits the tray and collects in the palm of the feeder who usually tosses the goods one at a time to watch us fight for it.

We jump for this food like savages. I am not proud of it but we don’t have the same luxuries of food availability as the feeders do. My brothers and sisters climb over my back and I climb over theirs. Unlucky for me, I am one of the smaller ones. Often I will be right there, mouth open wide in a big “O” to give the feeder a target. The feeder will toss it to me and at the last second a big stupid ugly koi will snatch it out of the air and land on me, plunging me down to the murky bottom.

Outside our brawl for food, the pond is a pretty calm place. In my free time I observe the feeders eat. They usually come in groups, though not always. If a spot isn’t open the visiting feeders will wait with urgency, making sure to be ready the absolute second their name is called.

When the feeders make their first plate, they attack the buffet with bulging eyes and great enthusiasm, kind of how we fight over pellets. They return to their table with an amalgamation of cuisines piled into a heap that seems to defy the laws of physics.

Their second plate is lighter and more selective, a quiet acknowledgment of an overly ambitious start.

Plates three through six get dark. Feeders appear defeated, yet they continue to return to the trough. If hunger brought them to the Premium Chinese Buffet, it is no longer what keeps them here. Some deeper instinct has taken control.

When the feeders finally leave, the enthusiasm and play they entered with has vanished. They have traded their smiles for exhausted sighs as they cradle the undersides of their swollen bellies. It appears their anticipation was more enjoyable than the act of the feast.

For a species with such abundance, one that discards food by the pound, they eat as though there will never be enough. As though the memory of scarcity lingers somewhere beneath the surface and that this meal will be their last opportunity to eat.

I have watched thousands of feeders pass by this pond from every walk of life, but regardless of who they are or why they come, the ritual remains the same. Whatever teaches a feeder to eat this way must happen long before they arrive at the Premium Chinese Buffet.

Group by group the feeders slunk out the door. Chairs are stacked. Blinds are let down. The clatter fades before a final flick and the world returns to darkness.

item.title: Just Read
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #95
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Don't trust book recommendations. Mine included.

The same book teaches two people completely different things. And a second read can feel like a totally different book. You are not the first person you were the first time around.

We learn from books as we are, not as they are.

And when you come to a book hungry for answers to your life's questions, your brain goes foraging in the words. It doesn't matter much which book, it matters that you are looking.

I firmly believe if you have a problem, you can take a good book, read a random page with intention, and you'll be closer to your solution.

So when non-readers ask me what to read, my answer is just read what sounds interesting to you. Your insights are in the act of reading rather than in the text.

item.title: Good Communities Provide, Great Communities Exclude
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #94
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Yuval Harari says that if you fight a chimp it'll eat your face off. But if 100v100 and the humans can coordinate a way to win. He uses this as an example to show that working in large numbers is what separates humans from the rest of the animal kingdom

So we humans make groups like families, neighborhoods, and companies because our collective is stronger than the individual parts. Naturally, we want to be a part of the best groups we can because the better our group, the more that is afforded to us.

My friend Ben once said to me that the best communities are the ones where everybody feels in debt to each other, but no one is keeping score. Communities like this lend each other money at no interest, host each other for free meals, and step up to provide when someone needs help.

Everyone wants to belong to these great communities, but it seems like there aren't many of them, so what makes them great and how do you create them?

The best communities are not those that can provide, but those that can exclude.

Harvard doesn't teach better physics than a community college, it sells a filter. They exclude who they find to be the dumb and poor so that when you say "I went to Harvard" people can infer a level of competency and/or wealth. If Harvard let anyone in, even if the quality of education stayed the same, the value of the degree would plummet.

All real groups have a process for keeping out undesirables, colleges call it admissions, countries call it borders, sports teams call it cuts. Whatever the name, successful groups understand that membership cannot be unlimited because the unqualified can asymmetrically tank the value of the community.

Imagine a basketball team that allowed one random person onto the roster. The team’s average talent would decline, but more importantly, the players who earned their spot would place less value on being part of the team. As Steve Jobs famously observed, "A" players want to work with "A" players. Once a group lowers its standards, its best members begin to leave, and the quality of the group deteriorates.

So you need an enforced opinionated standard.

I use the word enforced because those with the least to offer often have the most to gain from being affiliated with a high-status group. The weakest graduate from medical school is still a doctor and benefits from the reputation of the profession. This creates a constant incentive for people to join groups whose standards they have not earned. Without enforcement, the quality of the group falls toward the quality of its least qualified members.

I use the word opinionated because if you try to accommodate everyone, you stand for nothing. My ideal workout community is one where everyone wakes up early, pushes hard, and talks trash. Planet Fitness takes the opposite approach, installing a “lunk alarm” that goes off if you make a noise that could be seen as intimidating. Neither approach is objectively correct, but both create a clear culture that attracts people who want the same thing. If a gym tries to appeal equally to both ends of the intensity spectrum, it ends up appealing to neither.

I think most friendships are unintentional, formed through circumstance, proximity, or obligation. Great communities are different. They are built on mutual admiration and a willingness to give more than you take. They are difficult to create, but, as I have learned living away from home for the past five months, life is nothing without great people to experience it with. Building community is the highest-return investment a person can make.

item.title: Handmade is the New High Status
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #93
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
Making your own stuff used to be a sign you were poor, now only the rich can afford it.

When a family built their own furniture, sewed their own clothes, and cooked every meal from scratch, it was generally because they couldn't afford to pay someone who did it better. But with mass manufacturing, scale slashed the price of almost everything.

As the scarce becomes abundant, a new scarcity takes its place. It moved from the function of the object to the form of it. Rich people don't just want a table anymore, they want a table with a story.

Walk into the house of the poor and the home of the rich and you'll find the same objects. The couch, the table, the chairs. The difference is the poor bought their furniture from Ikea, and the rich made it with their dad.

Of course real skill takes years to build. Time is generally what the poor can't spare. So the status of making your own stuff flipped. It went from the thing you did because you had no option to the thing you do because you have all the options.

item.title: The Musk Exception
item.description: What I've Been Thinking About Lately #92
item.dc:creator: Dylan Brodeur
item.content:encoded:
I was working on a blog post called "Pick One" but ended up trashing it.

The premise was you should pick one priority for your life at any given point in time. This is important when your desires conflict, because often times splitting your efforts reduces your chances of success. Having one priority makes it easy to choose the best action.

For example, someone who wants to be both a writer and a content creator might benefit their content goals from scrolling social media to find ideas and engage with other creators. But these actions likely directly hinder their ability to write.

I thought this was solid advice but I couldn't square the fact that Elon Musk has 12 children, 5 incredibly successful companies, and posts 10k times a year on X. So who am I to say anything?

There's a popular logical fallacy called "Reductio ad Hitlerum" that says if you compare someone to Hitler, you've lost the argument. Leo Strauss coined this term because allusions to Hitler kept happening in debates. It would shut down constructive dialogue and was never a fair allusion.

As much as Hitler is evil, Elon is productive. They are exceptions. Because of this, they can't be used to explain normal people.

So I propose a new logical fallacy called The Musk Exception:

"If Elon is your only counterexample to a point, the point holds."
